Phylogenetic models of beta and alpha, with their sampling error

Source: R/trait_gradient.R
trait_gradient_phylo.Rd

Fits models of trait evolution to the \(\beta\), \(\alpha\) and mean trait of the species from trait_gradient(), with the sampling error of each value added to the phylogenetic covariance, and compares a model without phylogeny, Brownian motion and an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process by AIC. It tells whether the position of species along the gradient (\(\beta\)) and their difference from co-occurring species (\(\alpha\)) are conserved or labile.

Usage

trait_gradient_phylo(
  x,
  tree,
  responses = c("beta", "alpha", "mean"),
  models = c("white", "BM", "OU"),
  n_boot = 199,
  min_sites = 3
)

Arguments

x

Result of trait_gradient().

tree

Phylogeny (phylo) with branch lengths; its tips are matched to species by name.

responses

Which of "beta", "alpha" and "mean" to model.

models

Which of "white", "BM" and "OU" to fit.

n_boot

Number of bootstrap samples for the standard errors.

min_sites

Smallest number of sites of a species with a value (sites where it is alone do not count); species with fewer sites, or not in tree, are left out.

Value

An object of class mc_trait_gradient_phylo, a list with models (one row per response and model: response, model, mu, sigma2, a, half_life (\(\ln 2 / a\), in units of branch length), at_bound (an OU fit with \(a\) at a bound), loglik, n_par, aic and delta_aic within each response), data (one row per species used: values and standard errors) and tree (the tree pruned to those species).

Details

The standard error of each value comes from a bootstrap of the sites of each species: the sites (with their trait values and abundances) are resampled with replacement, and \(\bar t_i\), \(\beta_i\) and \(\alpha_i\) recomputed with the site means of the observed data (without the focal species, if so chosen). The site means are held fixed because the question is how well the sites of a species measure its position, not how the gradient itself would change.

For each response \(y\) the model is \(y \sim N(\mu 1, \sigma^2 C + S)\), with \(S\) the diagonal matrix of squared standard errors and \(C\) the identity ("white"), the shared branch lengths ("BM"), or, for "OU", the covariance of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with a root at \(\mu\) and strength \(a\), $$C_{ij} = e^{-a(d_i + d_j - 2 s_{ij})} \frac{1 - e^{-2 a s_{ij}}}{2a},$$ where \(d_i\) is the distance from the root to tip \(i\) and \(s_{ij}\) the length shared by \(i\) and \(j\). The parameters are estimated by restricted maximum likelihood, so AIC compares the covariance models with the same mean. Without the error term, the noise of species seen in few sites passes for evolution near the tips, which an OU process fits better: in simulations of \(\beta\) under Brownian motion (100 replicates, 30 species, 25 sites), AIC chose OU in 22 without the error term and in 9 with it.

\(a\) is bounded between \(10^{-3}\) and 50 divided by the height of the tree. At the lower bound OU is Brownian motion and at the upper bound it is the model without phylogeny; such fits are marked in at_bound and their half-life is NA. AIC differences among three models fitted to few species are unstable, and the bootstrap standard error of a species seen in \(n\) sites is biased low by about \(\sqrt{(n - 1)/n}\).

References

Ackerly, D. D., & Cornwell, W. K. (2007). A trait-based approach to community assembly: partitioning of species trait values into within- and among-community components. Ecology Letters, 10, 135–145. doi:10.1111/j.1461-0248.2006.01006.x

trait_gradient(), trait_ou() to simulate traits under these models.

Examples

set.seed(1)
tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(20)
sim <- simulate_metacommunity(landscape_implicit(15), species_traits(tree, lambda = 1),
                              competition_matrix(tree, "none"), n_steps = 100,
                              seed_steps = 1:5)
ind <- sample_individuals(sim, n = 5, local_adaptation = 0.5, intraspecific_sd = 1)
tg <- trait_gradient(ind, abundance = "abundance")
trait_gradient_phylo(tg, tree, n_boot = 99)
